name: Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 2 (CLN2 Disease, TPP1 Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1) due to biallelic CLN2 (TPP1) variants; the classic late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.
Typical presentation is language delay followed by seizures (often first afebrile seizures) and ataxia in a toddler or young child, then rapid motor and cognitive regression.
The combination of new-onset epilepsy plus a history of speech delay in a young child should specifically prompt consideration of CLN2.
Visual failure due to retinal degeneration tends to appear later in the course than in CLN3, but progresses to blindness.
CLN2 is the NCL subtype with an approved intracerebroventricular enzyme-replacement therapy (recombinant TPP1), making early recognition genuinely disease-altering.
Electron microscopy classically shows curvilinear inclusion bodies, contrasting with the granular osmiophilic deposits of CLN1 and the fingerprint profiles of CLN3.
Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating deficient TPP1 enzyme activity (dried blood spot or leucocytes) together with CLN2 molecular testing.
A standardised clinical rating scale is used to track motor and language decline and to monitor response to therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN2 disease is caused by deficiency of tripeptidyl peptidase 1, a lysosomal serine protease that sequentially removes tripeptides from the unblocked N-terminus of small polypeptides and also has endopeptidase activity at acidic pH. TPP1 is synthesised as an inactive proenzyme that is autocatalytically processed within the acidic lysosome to its mature form. Loss of TPP1 activity impairs lysosomal turnover of its protein substrates and leads to accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin storage material, notably including subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, forming curvilinear inclusions within neurons and other cells. The resulting lysosomal dysfunction drives neuroinflammation, synaptic loss and progressive neuronal death predominantly affecting the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and retina. Cerebellar involvement is early and prominent, correlating with the striking ataxia and later motor collapse, while cortical and retinal degeneration produce the cognitive decline, epilepsy and blindness. Residual enzyme activity influences phenotype, with rarer variants producing later-onset or predominantly ataxic or retinal presentations from the same gene.
additionalDifferentials: Other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, especially CLN1 (PPT1) and CLN3 (juvenile)
Late-infantile variant NCLs due to CLN5, CLN6, CLN7 (MFSD8) and CLN8
Progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Lafora and Unverricht-Lundborg disease
Autoimmune or infective encephalitis presenting with new seizures and regression
Late-onset GM2 gangliosidosis and other lysosomal disorders
Idiopathic epileptic encephalopathies before the neurodegenerative course declares itself
additionalInvestigations: TPP1 enzyme activity assay in dried blood spot, leucocytes or fibroblasts (deficient)
Molecular genetic testing of the CLN2 (TPP1) gene
Electron microscopy of skin, conjunctiva or lymphocytes for curvilinear inclusion bodies
MRI brain showing early cerebellar atrophy with later cerebral atrophy and periventricular white-matter signal change
Electroencephalography, including a characteristic photoparoxysmal response to low-frequency photic stimulation
Electroretinography and ophthalmological review documenting retinal degeneration and optic atrophy
Standardised CLN2 clinical rating scale to quantify and monitor motor and language decline
redFlags: New-onset unprovoked seizures in a young child with a preceding history of language delay
Progressive ataxia and myoclonus with loss of motor skills
Rapid regression of speech and cognition in the late-infantile period
Visual deterioration with retinal degeneration developing during the illness
Photoparoxysmal electroencephalographic response to slow photic stimulation
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic CLN2 progresses rapidly to loss of ambulation, speech and vision with death in childhood; intracerebroventricular enzyme-replacement therapy can slow motor and language decline when started early, altering the natural history.
pitfalls: Dismissing early language delay as isolated, then failing to link it to subsequent seizures and missing the CLN2 pattern.
Delaying TPP1 enzyme testing in a child with new epilepsy and regression, thereby losing the window for enzyme-replacement therapy.
Confusing CLN2 with CLN1 or CLN3, which have different enzymes, ultrastructure and management implications.
Overlooking the diagnostic value of the low-frequency photoparoxysmal electroencephalographic response.
Assuming visual failure must be early; in CLN2 it often follows the seizures and ataxia rather than preceding them.
